# PicoCalc Speech & Sound

*README.MD file mostly generated by Anthropic's Claude AI because Thomas Dzubin hates documenting code.  LOL*

A demo for the **ClockworkPi PicoCalc**, by **Thomas Dzubin**, exercising a
standalone software audio synthesis engine — sound effects and a formant-based
speech/singing voice — with no hardware beyond the PicoCalc's own speakers.
Written in C against the **Raspberry Pi Pico SDK** and the driver layer from
[`picocalc-text-starter`](https://github.com/BlairLeduc/picocalc-text-starter)
by **Blair Leduc** (LCD and south-bridge keyboard drivers) — vendored here
under [`picocalc-text-starter-main/`](picocalc-text-starter-main/).

```
main.c                        the top-level program: keyboard loop, help
                               screen, status line - calls into the two
                               modules below
picocalc_audio.c/.h            the synthesis engine: PWM-as-DAC output, a
                               noise/pulse voice with resonant filter and
                               envelope, and a phoneme sequencer
picocalc_sound_effects.c/.h    presets built on the engine: explosion,
                               gunshot, wind, surf, raindrops
picocalc_speech.c/.h           presets built on the engine: vowels, spoken
                               words, singing
CMakeLists.txt                 builds the firmware, reusing picocalc-text-starter-main/
                               drivers/* for the LCD and keyboard
desktop/                       Desktop (SDL2) build, Windows and Linux: CMakeLists.txt + a small shim
                               that stands in for the PicoCalc's LCD, keyboard and
                               PWM audio hardware
pico_sdk_import.cmake           standard Pico SDK locator (copied from the
                               starter)
picocalc-text-starter-main/    vendored driver layer (see License; do not edit)
LICENSE, CHANGELOG.md           MIT licence; version history
```

## What it does

On startup the screen shows a static list of controls and a "LAST: ..."
status line that updates every time a key below plays something. There is no
other UI — this project is a tuning/demo harness for the audio engine, not an
instrument or a game.

| Key | Plays |
|-----|-------|
| `E` | **Explosion** — a bright crack, a low-pitched noise body and a pitched-down sub layer |
| `G` | **Gunshot** — crack, report and a fast downward-sweeping muzzle blast |
| `W` | Toggle **wind** — sustained stereo band-passed noise, two mismatched LFOs so it never settles into a static hiss |
| `Z` | Toggle **surf** — built like the wind preset but a broadband roar on a slower swell |
| `X` | **Raindrops** — a short one-shot scatter of falling-water sounds, randomised per call |
| `V` | A **sung vowel** ("ah") at a fixed pitch |
| `H` | Says **"hello"** |
| `J` | Says **"goodbye"** |
| `K` | Says **"PicoCalc"** |
| `S` | Sings **"hello"** an octave above its normal speaking pitch |
| `1` | Says a full **sentence** — "Hello, I am a PicoCalc. I can talk. Can you understand me?" |
| `4` `5` `6` `7` `8` | A **sine**, **triangle**, **square**, **sawtooth** and **pulse** wave, all at the same 500 Hz — hear the engine's raw oscillator shapes on their own |
| `ESC` | **Stop** all sound and reset to the ready-for-input state |
| `Q` | Stop all sound and **leave for the PicoCalc UF2 Loader** menu. It asks the loader for its menu through the watchdog scratch registers (constants in `loader_const.h`); with no loader installed the program just restarts, and on a PC it closes |
| `~` (SHIFT + backtick) | Reboot into **BOOTSEL** (USB drive) mode |

Expect a **Speak & Spell / SAM** sort of voice from the speech keys — that's
inherent to a pulse-plus-three-formants model, not a tuning shortfall.

## The engine

`picocalc_audio.c/.h` is the reusable part: a PWM slice run as a ~12-bit DAC,
one sample per PWM period, with noise generation, a resonant band-pass filter
and an ADSR-style envelope per voice, plus a phoneme sequencer that glides a
voice between formant targets over time. `pcaudio_init(true)` starts its
sample-rate interrupt on core 1, out of reach of the interrupt masking
`lcd_blit()` does on the drawing core (core 0), so screen updates never click
or stutter the audio.

`picocalc_sound_effects.c/.h` and `picocalc_speech.c/.h` are both just presets
built on top of that engine — plain `pcaudio_patch_t` configurations and
phoneme tables — split into their own files so a project can take the engine
plus only the one it needs.

## Adding a new spoken word

`picocalc_speech.c` currently speaks three words ("hello", "goodbye",
"PicoCalc"), each a hand-written `pcaudio_phoneme_t[]` — a sequence of vocal
targets (formants, pitch, loudness) the engine glides smoothly between.
`picocalc_speech.h` has the building blocks for writing more:

- All 10 steady-state American-English vowels (`PCAUDIO_VOWEL_*`), plus a
  comment mapping the 5 English diphthongs to onset/offset vowel pairs.
- Named formant constants for consonants: place-of-articulation loci shared
  by the stops and nasals, the four fricative noise colours, both liquids
  (`/l/`, `/r/`), and both glides (`/w/`, `/y/`).

Each of `hello_seq`, `goodbye_seq` and `picocalc_seq` in `picocalc_speech.c`
is a heavily-commented worked example — the `/l/` in "hello" and the stop
consonants in "goodbye"/"PicoCalc" are a good place to start copying from.

## Building

You need the Raspberry Pi Pico SDK toolchain (arm-none-eabi-gcc, CMake,
Ninja) — exactly what `picocalc-text-starter` already builds with.

### With the Raspberry Pi Pico VS Code extension (easiest)

Open this folder (`PicoCalc-Speech/`) in VS Code with the *Raspberry Pi Pico*
extension installed, then **Compile** (or *Run > Compile Project*). The
`CMakeLists.txt` here uses the same `pico-vscode.cmake` preamble as the
starter, so it picks up your installed SDK 2.2.0 / toolchain automatically.

### From a terminal

```bash
# point at your Pico SDK checkout (SDK 2.2.0; install per the Raspberry Pi
# "C/C++ SDK" docs, or let the VS Code Pico extension manage it)
export PICO_SDK_PATH=/path/to/pico-sdk

cmake -B build -G Ninja
cmake --build build
```

The result is **`build/speech-<chip>.uf2`** (`<chip>` is `RP2350` or `RP2040`, matching the board), which the build also copies to
this folder as **`speech-RP2040.uf2`** or
**`speech-RP2350.uf2`** (depending on the board), so both chips'
builds can sit side by side.

> If your PicoCalc uses a **Pico 2 / RP2350**, configure with
> `-DPICO_BOARD=pico2` (or set it in the VS Code extension). For a Pico W use
> `-DPICO_BOARD=pico_w`.

### On Windows

The same program also runs on a Windows PC through a small SDL2 layer in
[`desktop/`](desktop/). It stands in for the LCD and keyboard, and it emulates
the PWM sample interrupt that drives the sound engine: SDL's audio callback
plays the part of the PWM hardware, so `picocalc_audio.c` runs unmodified at
its normal 22050 Hz. From an MSYS2 UCRT64 shell with SDL2 installed:

```bash
cmake -S desktop -B build-windows -G Ninja
ninja -C build-windows
```

The result is **`speech-Windows.exe`** in this folder. SDL2 is linked
statically, so it is a single file with no `SDL2.dll`. `~` simply closes the
program.

### Linux

The same source builds on Linux with the SDL2 development package installed
(for example `sudo apt install libsdl2-dev`). Unlike the Windows build, SDL2 is
**not** linked in statically: the program links `libSDL2` dynamically, and the
build copies that library next to the executable as `libSDL2-2.0.so.0`, where
the executable finds it through an `$ORIGIN` run-path. Keep the two files
together.

    cmake -S desktop -B build-linux
    cmake --build build-linux

Output: `speech-Linux` and `libSDL2-2.0.so.0` in the top-level folder.

## Flashing

1. Hold **BOOTSEL** on the Pico while plugging in USB (or, if the program is
   already running, press **`~`** / SHIFT + backtick — it reboots straight
   into BOOTSEL).
2. Copy `build/speech-<chip>.uf2` onto the `RPI-RP2` / `RP2350` drive.
3. The PicoCalc restarts into the program.

## Hardware notes / pins

All pin assignments come from the reused starter drivers, except audio which
is driven directly by `picocalc_audio.c` rather than the starter's own audio
driver:

| Function              | Pins / bus                                              |
|-----------------------|----------------------------------------------------------|
| LCD (ST7365P)         | `spi1` – SCK 10, MOSI 11, MISO 12, CS 13, DC 14, RST 15  |
| Keyboard south-bridge  | `i2c1` – SDA 6, SCL 7, address `0x1F`, FIFO reg `0x09`   |
| Audio (PWM-as-DAC)    | GP26 (left) and GP27 (right)                              |

The keyboard FIFO is polled directly with `sb_read_keyboard()` so the program
sees raw press/release events. Because of that it does **not** call
`picocalc_init()` — that would start the starter's background keyboard poll,
which drains the same FIFO.

## Known limitations

- **One voice per effect slot at a time.** Overlapping demo keys (e.g.
  triggering an explosion while wind is already running) is only as good as
  the engine's voice-stealing behaviour — this is a tuning/demo harness, not
  a mixer.
- **No tests / CI.** Build and flash are manual.

### Third-party

`picocalc-text-starter-main/` is a vendored copy of
[**picocalc-text-starter**](https://github.com/BlairLeduc/picocalc-text-starter)
by Blair Leduc (the LCD and south-bridge keyboard drivers). It is **not**
relicensed by this project — it keeps its own MIT license at
[`picocalc-text-starter-main/LICENSE`](picocalc-text-starter-main/LICENSE),
Copyright © 2025 Blair Leduc. The Raspberry Pi Pico SDK it builds against is
licensed separately by Raspberry Pi Ltd. (BSD-3-Clause).

The vendored copy is unchanged except for **one small fix** in
`picocalc-text-starter-main/drivers/fat32.c`: `get_next_free_cluster()` now
advances its search hint past the cluster it just handed out; without that,
every later allocation re-scans the clusters already given out, and a long
sequential write to the SD card looks hung. Everything else is exactly as
downloaded.
